nameStory: The alternating dog lichen gets its curious name from the finger-like lobes that alternate along its edges, creating a distinctive pattern unlike other dog lichens. The 'dog' part comes from the old belief that these lichens could cure rabies in dogs, though we now know they have no medicinal properties.
description: Alternating dog lichen is a medium-sized foliose (leaf-like) lichen that forms broad, flat patches on soil and moss. It has distinctive blue-gray to brownish lobes that spread out like fingers, with the characteristic alternating pattern along the edges that gives it its name. The lichen can grow to about 4-6 inches across, forming colonies that look like miniature lettuce leaves scattered across the forest floor.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms broad, flat, leaf-like lobes that lie close to the ground, feeling somewhat papery when dry but becoming more pliable when moist

idTips.label: Edge Pattern
idTips.description: The lobes have a distinctive alternating finger-like pattern along their margins - this is the key identifying feature that separates it from other dog lichens

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Blue-gray to brownish-gray on top when dry, becoming more vibrant blue-green when wet; underneath is pale with distinctive dark veins

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Smooth to slightly wrinkled upper surface that feels soft and velvety to the touch, without the bumpy texture of many other lichens

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always grows on soil, moss, or decaying organic matter on the forest floor - never on rocks or tree bark

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual lobes typically 2-4 inches long, with entire colonies reaching 4-6 inches across when mature

habitat: Look for alternating dog lichen in moist, shaded areas of deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly in areas with rich, well-drained soil. It thrives in the understory where it gets filtered light, often growing among mosses and leaf litter in valleys and on gentle slopes. You'll most commonly find it in mature forests with consistent moisture levels.

seasonality.spring: Most vibrant after spring rains when the blue-green colors are at their brightest and the texture becomes noticeably softer and more flexible.
seasonality.summer: May appear somewhat dried and gray during hot, dry periods, but the alternating lobe pattern remains clearly visible for identification.
seasonality.fall: Often partially hidden under falling leaves but still identifiable; the contrast between the lichen and colorful autumn leaves can make it easier to spot.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible under light snow cover and may show enhanced colors during winter thaws when moisture levels are high.

funFact: This lichen is actually two organisms living as one - the blue-green color comes from cyanobacteria living inside the fungal body that can pull nitrogen directly from the air, essentially fertilizing the forest floor as the lichen grows and decomposes.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other dog lichens, especially the common dog pelt lichen, but the alternating finger-like pattern along the edges is unique - think 'alternating fingers' to remember the key difference from the more evenly-lobed relatives.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'dog lichen' for this entire group comes from medieval folklore about curing rabid dog bites, but modern science shows these lichens are harmless to handle and have no medicinal properties - they're simply beautiful examples of nature's partnerships.
compareHints: Unlike the more common dog pelt lichen which has evenly-spaced, rounded lobes, alternating dog lichen has its distinctive alternating finger-like projections along the edges. It's also generally smaller than many-fruited pelt lichen and lacks the prominent reproductive structures often seen in that species. The alternating pattern is truly unique among New England's pelt lichens.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the pelt lichens, scaly pelt is the only one in New England with prominent phyllidia scattered across its surface.

Among the many pelt lichens in New England, horizontal pelt lichen is unique for its completely prostrate growth habit - it never curls up at the edges like dog pelt lichen or forms the ruffled, frilly margins of freckled pelt lichen.
Distinguished from dog pelt lichen by having many more fruiting structures along the edges rather than just a few large ones.

Among the many pelt lichens in New England, dog pelt lichen stands out for its preference for growing directly on soil rather than trees, and its particularly well-defined dark veining on a pale underside.
Among the pelt lichens, ruffled freckled pelt stands out for its notably bumpy, textured surface and strongly ruffled edges.
Unlike all other pelt lichens in New England, Eastern Waterfan is the only one that lives in water rather than on soil, rocks, or trees in terrestrial habitats.
Among the pelt lichens, freckled pelt is the only one with distinctive dark green cephalodia (freckles), making identification fairly straightforward.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a smooth surface, peppered pelt is distinguished by its dark spotted pattern.
Among its pelt lichen relatives, sheepish pelt lichen is distinguished by its uniquely woolly surface texture - most other Peltigera species have smooth or slightly wrinkled surfaces.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a relatively uniform surface with veins on the underside, concentric pelt lichen displays obvious ring patterns on top.
